Regular Council Meeting
CITY OF SOLANA BEACH
ACTION AGENDA
The Action Agenda of the City Council Meeting is a document provided immediately following the Council Meeting in order for staff and the public to be aware of the business transacted and actions taken by Council. This is a preliminary draft and not a public record. The meeting's legal record is the Minutes approved by the City Council.
Solana Beach City Council, Successor Agency to the Redevelopment Agency, Public Financing Authority, & Housing Authority
Joint REGULAR Meeting
Wednesday, April 11, 2012
6:00
P.M.
City Hall / Council Chambers
635 S. Highway 101, Solana Beach, California
Public Meeting Access
The Regular Meetings of the City Council are scheduled for the 2nd and 4th Wednesdays and are broadcast live on Cox Communications-Channel 19, Time Warner-Channel 24 (analog) or Channel 131 (digital) , and AT&T U-verse Channel 99. The video taping of meetings are maintained as a permanent record and contain a detailed account of the proceedings. Council meeting tapings are archived and available for viewing on the City's website.
Agenda Materials
A full City Council agenda packet including relative supporting documentation is available at City Hall, the Solana Beach Branch Library (157 Stevens Ave.), La Colonia Community Ctr., Fletcher Cove Lifeguard station, and online www.cityofsolanabeach.org. Agendas are posted at least 72 hours prior to the meeting. Writings and documents regarding an agenda of an open session meeting, received after the official posting, and distributed to the Council for consideration, will be made available for public viewing at the same time. In addition, items received at least 1 hour 30 minutes prior to the meeting time will be uploaded online with the courtesy agenda posting. Materials submitted for consideration should be forwarded to the City Clerk's department 858-720-2400. The designated location for viewing public documents is the City Clerk's office at City Hall during normal business hours.
Speakers
Please submit a speaker slip to the City Clerk prior to the meeting, or the announcement of the Section/Item, to provide public comment. Allotted times for speaking are outlined on the speaker's slip for each agenda section: Oral Communications, Consent, Public Hearings and Staff Reports.
American Disabilities Act Title 2
In compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, persons with a disability may request an agenda in appropriate alternative formats as required by Section 202. Any person with a disability who requires a modification or accommodation in order to participate in a meeting should direct such request to the City Clerk's office (858) 720-2400 at least 72 hours prior to the meeting.
As a courtesy to all meeting attendees, please set cellular phones and pagers to silent mode
and engage in conversations outside the Council Chambers.

C.1.
San Onofre Nuclear Generating Station. (File 0230-51)
Recommendation: That the City Council
1.
Hear the item, receive public discussion, and provide direction as appropriate
David Ott, City Manager, introduced the item.
Councilmember Heebner stated that this issue is within the Council’s purview to discuss, and that one of their jobs as Councilmembers was public safety.
Sharon Hoffman asked Council to consider Councilmember Heebner’s point, that Solana Beach was in the danger zone, that the words from City governments could make a difference, and urged the Council to put their voice behind the citizens and other officials who were speaking out against San Onofre.
Gene Stone stated that Fukushima citizens believed their government and officials who stated that the plant was safe, that Fukushima was continuing to meltdown, that there could be worldwide radiation from the disaster, that he believed San Onofre made changes without the NRC approval, and asked Council to support the demand to find out the problems with both reactors before restarting either.
Ace Hoffman stated that these reactors were different than the ones in Fukushima, but that the steam generators were the damaged equipment at this time, that a ground shake might be a bad thing and a low proximity might be bad in a tsunami, that local communities in Japan were preventing the federal government in Japan from reopening the generators at Fukushima, and urged Council to examine and discover the holes in San Onofre’s owner’s statements.
Richard Moore stated that restarting the generators without knowing what the problems were did not make good sense, that nuclear energy was vital energy and generally good and necessary, that once Council passed this resolution they could be drawn into a national debate on nuclear power, Council’s time would be better spent on other issues, that radiation was not the cause of mortality in Fukushima, that he hoped that they could move forward without negating nuclear power as an option, and that the distrust of the nuclear regulatory commission needed to be addressed.
Crystal Coleman stated that nuclear power was a crime against humanity, displayed pictures of deformities, and said hat nuclear radiation effects did not show up until twenty to thirty years after exposure, that exposure to nuclear radiation caused cancer and birth defects, that there would be no need for an escape route if there were a disaster because there would be nowhere to go, that a primary importance should be the health and safety of children and the planet, that Fukushima was a wake up call, and that a plan to phase out San Onofre was needed.
Gary Hedrick (time donated by Helen Bourne) stated that he and his wife started an environmental group called San Clemente Green, that they were approached by workers at San Onofre who were discriminated against for reporting safety violations, that there was not a strong response from NRC about issues that preceeded the plant shut down, the testing of the generators were being skipped, a chain reaction of tubes bursting at San Onofre was close, that units two and three are being treated separately even though they were the same generators, and showed a map displaying where Solana Beach was in relation to the fallout zone.
Dick Eiden said he was a resident of Vista, urged Council to watch the frontline show about Fukushima, elected officials too easily took the word of the nuclear industry and the agencies who were supposed to regulate them, that promises of safe, clean, cheap energy had been proven to be wrong, that public officials must put safety ahead of profits, and suggested that Council join other City Councils and City officials to study the issue.
Jenifer Massey stated that human error had been a factor in many disasters and that natural disasters could not be controlled, that San Onofre was only equipped to handle a 7.0 earthquake and that there was a great chance that the area could experience one in excessof that magnitude, that the evacuation route was impractical, that the assumption that Interstate 5 would not be affected was unrealistic, that a disaster of this scale would be financially devastating, and that wind would route the nuclear radiation all over the country.
Grace Van Thillo stated that they met with officials from the NRC and questioned their steps to deal with the closed reactors, that given traffic realities the evacuation would be next to impossible, that the aging plant during re-licensing would not be held accountable to new reactor standards, and that Council’s actions would send a strong message to determine the root cause and extent of the damage, Edison’s repair plans, and cost of repairs.
Swedine Hurt stated that she had a degree in biochemistry and a degree in business, that the NRC commissioned a cracked tube report in 1982 that showed a meltdown of San Onofre would result in 27,000 fatalities per reactor, 23,000 injuries per reactor, 18,000 cancer deaths per reactor, that the population of southern California had one and a half times, that it was now known that radiation caused cancer three times more than assumed in 1982, that the new figures would result in 243,000 fatalities per reactor, 207,000 injuries per reactor, and 162,000 per reactor cancer deaths per reactor, that fetus’ were 1000 times more vulnerable than adults and children were 20 times more vulnerable than adults, and that at the Nuclear Security Summit it was stated last month that Fukushima’s reactor four was about to collapse which would result in a meltdown 84 times worse than Chernobyl.
Roger Johnson (Lori Johnson donated time) stated that the issue was a moral issue, that San Onofre had become the poster child for everything wrong in the nuclear power industry, that there had been two studies in the last decade that determined children who grew up near a nuclear doubled their chance of developing childhood leukemia, that there were regular radiation releases ejecting radioactive substances into the atmosphere and ocean, and that low level emissions were allowed but they were only required to report once a year so they could release their whole allowable radiation in one day and still be within the law.
Jeff Steinmetz stated that he had no problem with people making a profit, that he never would have purchased a house in San Clemente had he known what he now knows, reviewed his experience of a false alarm at San Onofre a couple of years ago, that at the time there was nothing on the news and he could not get through to 911, that the false alarm was caused by rain accessing an alarm which did not give him a lot of faith in the engineers at San Onofre, that the ISO's 2012 release said that the power produced there was not needed, and that the NRC was not protecting people and not doing their job.
Patti Davis stated that she never worried about nuclear power until she saw the disaster at Fukushima, showed a chart demonstrating the excess of power in California that would be unaffected with the absence of nuclear power, that she had a friend in Japan who said everyone in Japan was afraid of the rain because of what radiation could be in it, and that the risk of San Onofre was not needed.
Donna Gilmore handed out a document and stated that the news article that was about employees of the plant being punished for reporting safety concerns, that she had learned that San Onofre had the worst safety record in the entire country, that the power it produced was not required, and that the problem generator had been installed less than a year before despite that fact that it was supposed to last forty years.
Sandy Stiassni stated that he was an advocate for sustainability and public safety, that the aging San Onofre power plant had a history of troubling violations, that there was no safe evacuation plan in case of a meltdown, that Council should carefully study all impacts of the plant on its citizens, and urged Council to speak out to decommission SONGS and remove all waste.
Torgen Johnson (time donated by Colleen Dietzel) presented a powerpoint (on file) including a report by Friends of the Earth by Fairland Associates, and stated that Solana Beach was in the fifty mile disaster radius which made the issue local, that he bought a Geiger counter and found radioactivity in the milk in his fridge, that there was no information from of San Onofre during the blackout in September, that the NRC and Edison told everyone that they were safe but the USGS said something different, and urged Council to send a clear message.
Lane Sharman (time donated by Peter House) said that he was arrested forty years ago for witnessing a protest as a result of bombing railroads in Vietnam, that it was relevant because they were destroying a country to save it, that in respect to energy the benefit did not justify the risk, that the environment was being destroyed in order to save the economy, that nuclear energy did not produce CO2 so it was considered clean energy even though it was a risk to the environment, and that there was plenty of energy on the grid and that gas energy could be imported, if needed.
Bart Zeigler stated that the San Onofre facilities were old and decrepit, that the continuing operation posed an unacceptable risk to health and safety, that the three mile Island event was partially due to human error but also one of the nations top engineers, that the San Onofre had the same circuitry that was a flaw in that power station, that the fuel stored in the facility was not safely stored, that the pools storing the waste should be a priority, and listed the effects of radiation.
Chris Abel, outreach manager of San Onofre, reviewed that status of the plant, and stated that their number one priority was protecting the public and employees, that Unit 2 was shut down on January 9th for normal refueling and maintenance, that they detected a very small steam leak which released a small amount of radiation and calculated it to be 200,000 times less than a chest x-ray, that they were not required to shut the generator down but did so in an abundance of caution, that 129 of the 19,000 generator tubes showed excessive wear and that 8 of the tubes did not pass the test which they immediately reported to the NRC, that they sent a plan to NRC on how to address the problem, and that the NRC sent a confimation action letter agreeing with their findings.
Councilmember Campbell asked Mr. Abel what was the plan in the event of an earthquake.
Mr. Abel explained that the plant was built to withstand twice the sizable event, that the nuclear industry earthquakes were measured by peak ground acceleration, and that the Richter Scale did not take speed or distance into account.
Councilmember Campbell asked what the plan was in case of a disaster due to human error.
Mr. Abel stated that he could not speculate as it would depend on the details of what happened.
Councilmember Nichols asked how much energy San Onofre provided.
Mr. Abel said that San Onofre provided 2200 megawatts which was enough for 1.1 million average homes and that southern Californians received 19% of their power from nuclear energy.
Councilmember Nichols asked Mr. Abel to address the claims that San Onofre had the worst safety record in the United States.
Mr. Abel reiterated that they took safety very seriously, that the NRC had addressed all issues, and that he was not aware of any official rankings.
Councilmember Nichols asked how the age of San Onofre compared to other plants.
Mr. Abel stated that he was not an expert on other plants, but that although the plant was over forty years old, the equipment they were using was not forty years old.
Councilmember Campbell questioned Mr. Abel about the graphs displaying the excess power in California showing that nuclear power was in excess.
Mr. Abel stated that the question would be for SDGE.
Councilmember Heebner read that the report ranking San Onofre as the worst in the United States was produced by the NRC in 2011, and asked Mr. Abel to address the report.
Mr. Abel stated that the NRC had investigated all of those issues and addressed them.
Gary Martin stated that he wanted to know how San Onofre would address a meltdown to get the millions of people out of the area and where would they go.
Councilmember Heebner stated that she and Councilmember Nichols went to Dana Point to hear the NRC response, that both of their state Senators were concerned about the San Onofre plant, that they learned that the safety standards for new plants were not the same as old ones, that the San Onofre plant could not be built today, that SONGS and Diablo Canyon plants were the only two plants in the Country located in the highest seismic hazard areas, as of March 2011, that a study on the preparedness of the plants revealed that the NRC’s safety approach was incomplete for dealing with the unexpected and that the report made recommendations called "Lessons from Fukushima," that the 30 mile radius was based on the amount of dollars that the nuclear industry could absorb and not related to safety concerns, changes could be implemented over five years, that she hoped Council could give the Senators and Chair support, that there were a number of problems including who oversaw the plant and their motives were not related to the impact on peopl. She said that the dome shells were created for protection but that they were penetrated in order to put steam generators into the plant, that she suggested a letter or resolution from Council to the NRC with copies to Boxer and Feinstein including the need to modify re-licensing policies in order to assure a full re-examination of the design basis elements, including earthquake and tsunami hazards, operational issues, plant security, emergency preparedness, and spent fuel storage options. She said that it should also include a mechanism for appointing the NRC commissioners and to review the risk analysis that the NRC uses to assure it accurately assesses public risk factors.
Councilmember Nichols also attended the meeting last Friday, said that the chair Gregory Jesko? seemed like a down to earth person, his concerns were the same as everyone in the room and that was public safety, that as Council they were charged with public safety, that the debate is not on nuclear energy policy but on the concerns of what could happen in a natural or man made disaster, that it was natural to consider local concerns after Fukishima, that the generators that are offline right now would not be allowed to start back up until the issue are addressed, that he wanted to support Gregory Jesko and Senators who were stating their concerns, and that he agreed with drafting a letter.
Mayor Kellejian stated that the agenda was void of any comment or study on the issue that would give the Council the tools to make a decision on the matter, that the City did not have the tools to investigate a situation of this magnitude, that there were a lot of questions that needed to be answered, and that he could not make a decision on the subject without actual concrete information.
Councilmember Campbell clarified that Councilmember Heebner’s motion would not request the decommission of the plant but would provide support on the federal level to look at the issue harder and respond to the concerns, that he agreed that more information was needed before supporting decommissioning the plant, and that he was convinced the Council should take a position on the issue in the framework of what Councilmember Heebner suggested regarding drafting letters of concern.
Deputy Mayor Roberts said that he visited SONGS and learned that the land that it was built on was rented from the Army, that as soon as the plant lost its license that the plant reverted back to Camp Pendleton, SONGS was the only power plant bisected by a freeway, that he did not want to get into the debate about the spent fuel and other complex issues such as the fuel tanks, that there were some issues he thought needed to be addressed such as the corrosion along the sea wall, and that he would support a letter as long as it was tightly crafted to stick to the public safety concerns and to support their national leaders to make sure they do what they were charged to do which was to help Council protect residents in Solana Beach.
Mayor Kellejian stated that he would not support any action at this time due to lack of factual information, would abstain from voting, and would reserve his final vote until after the letter was crafted.
Councilmember Heebner clarified her motion to send a letter to Chair Yazko, with copies to the Senators, supporting the NRC to modify re-licensing policies in order to assure full re-examination of the plant, to support Senators in their call to implement the short term recommendations in the Lessons from Fukishima task report and develop a feasible plan to implement the long term recommendations, ask federal officials to review mechanism for employing NRC commissioners, ask federal officials to review NRC risk factors to ensure they meet public safety needs, and specifically mentioning the NRC evacuation plan.
Deputy Mayor Roberts stated that in order to keep the Council united, he asked the Mayor if he would reconsider his position and support the motion.
Mayor Kellejian stated that there were things in the motion he needed to review, that he was not voting against it, but that he needed to see the final product before voting.
